**CPU vs. GPU – the big picture**

| Feature | CPU (Central Processing Unit) | GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) |
|---------|------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose “brain” of the computer – handles everything from the OS to user apps. | Specialized hardware for rendering graphics, but now also used for highly parallel scientific and machine‑learning workloads. |
| **Core count** | Few (2–32 in consumer CPUs, up to 64+ in servers). | Hundreds to thousands (e.g., 2,560 cores in an NVIDIA RTX 3090). |
| **Core design** | Complex, high‑performance cores with deep pipelines, large caches, branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution. | Simple, lightweight cores optimized for throughput; each core does the same operation on many data elements. |
| **Execution model** | **Serial / few‑threaded**: one instruction stream per core, but can run many threads via hyper‑threading. | **Massively parallel**: thousands of threads run the same instruction (SIMD/SIMT). |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches, sophisticated memory controllers, low latency. | Smaller per‑core caches, larger shared memory, higher bandwidth memory (GDDR6/7). |
| **Typical workloads** | Control flow heavy tasks: OS, web browsers, office apps, database queries, gaming logic. | Data‑parallel tasks: rendering pixels/vertices, matrix math, convolution, deep‑learning inference/training, scientific simulations. |
| **Latency vs. throughput** | Optimized for low latency – quick response to a single request. | Optimized for high throughput – many operations per second, even if each takes longer. |
| **Power efficiency** | Balanced for a mix of tasks; power scales with clock speed and core count. | Very power‑hungry when fully utilized; but for the work it does, it can be more energy‑efficient than a CPU doing the same thing. |
| **Programming model** | Traditional CPU programming (C/C++, Java, etc.) with multi‑threading libraries. | Requires GPU‑aware APIs (CUDA, OpenCL, DirectX, Vulkan, Metal) or higher‑level frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch). |
| **Flexibility** | Can run any code; handles branching, recursion, complex data structures. | Best for regular, predictable patterns; struggles with irregular branching or pointer‑heavy code. |

### Why the difference matters

- **Speed**: For a single pixel or vertex, a GPU can finish in a few clock cycles because all its cores work together. A CPU would need to serialize that work across a handful of cores.
- **Parallelism**: GPUs shine when you have thousands of identical operations (e.g., multiply‑accumulate in a neural net). CPUs excel when you need to make decisions, handle I/O, or run a single complex algorithm.
- **Cost & Power**: A CPU can do everything but may be slower for graphics or ML. A GPU can do those tasks fast but is not a general replacement for a CPU.

### Modern trends

- **Unified memory**: GPUs now share memory with CPUs (e.g., NVIDIA’s Unified Memory, AMD’s Heterogeneous System Architecture), easing data transfer.
- **AI acceleration**: GPUs (and specialized ASICs like TPUs) dominate deep‑learning training and inference because of their parallel math capabilities.
- **Hybrid systems**: Many laptops and desktops use an integrated GPU (iGPU) for everyday tasks and a discrete GPU for heavy workloads.

---

**Bottom line:**  
A CPU is a versatile, low‑latency processor for general tasks, while a GPU is a massively parallel, high‑throughput engine optimized for data‑parallel workloads like graphics rendering and machine learning. They complement each other rather than replace one another.
